implementation_notes: Scala has first-class lazy initialization: `lazy val x = expr` evaluates on first access and at most once by language guarantee - Scala 3 implements it with a bitmask state machine and CAS (the reference describes the 0..3 states and the cancellation-safety rationale of SIP-20) - and `object` declarations are initialized on first access under JVM class-initialization semantics. The C++ structure therefore maps onto a keyword, and the remaining decisions are about recursion and about non-lazy vals that initialize during construction.
code_sketch:
object Registry {                       // initialized on first access
  private val providers = ListBuffer.empty[Provider]
  def register(p: Provider): Unit = providers += p
}

lazy val config: Config = Config.load()  // computed once, on first use
pitfalls: Recursive lazy vals are undefined and typically deadlock (the reference states the behaviour is undefined); a lazy val whose initializer needs the object being constructed is a design error, not a runtime problem to be tuned.

A plain val initializes during construction, including while a superclass constructor runs, so an override can be observed as null before the subclass body executes - the initialization-order FAQ problem that lazy val fixes, at the cost of a check on every read.
lazy val adds a synchronized/volatile check to every access (only limited cases are optimized back to a plain field), so hot paths should read it into a local once.
A failure while initializing an object surfaces as ExceptionInInitializerError and poisons the object for the rest of the process.
